variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Consistent hashing is a placement technique for choosing an owner from a changing set of nodes. It hashes both keys and node positions into the same ordered space. A key belongs to the first node position reached while walking around that space.
variants.prompt: Match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Hash space
pairs.detail: A deterministic hash turns each key and node identity into a position.
pairs.explanation: A deterministic hash turns each key and node identity into a position. The production hash space is large; lesson diagrams use a small circle so ownership is visible.

pairs.label: Token
pairs.detail: A token is one position owned by a physical node.
pairs.explanation: A token is one position owned by a physical node. One node may own many tokens, which split its responsibility into smaller ranges.

pairs.label: Successor owner
pairs.detail: Hash the key, find the first token at or after that position, and wrap to the first token when the lookup passes the end of the space.
pairs.explanation: Hash the key, find the first token at or after that position, and wrap to the first token when the lookup passes the end of the space.

pairs.label: Token range
pairs.detail: The interval after one token and through the next token shares an owner.
pairs.explanation: The interval after one token and through the next token shares an owner. Membership change transfers ranges, not arbitrary individual keys.

variants.hint:
Hash space: A deterministic hash turns each key and node identity into a position.

Token: A token is one position owned by a physical node.

Successor owner: Hash the key, find the first token at or after that position, and wrap to the first token when the lookup passes the end of the space.

Token range: The interval after one token and through the next token shares an owner.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Keeping these boundaries clear helps you find the place to change when the system behaves unexpectedly.

pairs.label: Publish the new token map
pairs.detail: Give the membership view an epoch or version so stale routers can be detected instead of silently disagreeing about ownership.
pairs.explanation: Give the membership view an epoch or version so stale routers can be detected instead of silently disagreeing about ownership.

pairs.label: Stream the changing ranges
pairs.detail: Copy or rebuild the affected data while the old owner can still serve it.
pairs.explanation: Copy or rebuild the affected data while the old owner can still serve it. Bound bandwidth so rebalancing does not consume the live request budget.

pairs.label: Switch authoritative routing
pairs.detail: Move reads and writes under an explicit handoff contract.
pairs.explanation: Move reads and writes under an explicit handoff contract. Define how concurrent writes, retries, and a failed transfer are reconciled.

pairs.label: Retire the old ownership
pairs.detail: Delete old copies only after integrity, replica count, and request routing are proven for the new map.
pairs.explanation: Delete old copies only after integrity, replica count, and request routing are proven for the new map.

pairs.label: Ring-based consistent hashing
pairs.detail: Use a ring when keys or requests need stable affinity while a node set changes and the system can operate token metadata plus controlled movement.
pairs.explanation: Use a ring when keys or requests need stable affinity while a node set changes and the system can operate token metadata plus controlled movement.

pairs.label: Fixed hash slots
pairs.detail: Use a fixed slot space when operators should move named slot ranges explicitly.
pairs.explanation: Use a fixed slot space when operators should move named slot ranges explicitly. Redis Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots and states that it does not use consistent hashing.

pairs.label: Round robin or least request
pairs.detail: Use ordinary load balancing when requests do not need key affinity.
pairs.explanation: Use ordinary load balancing when requests do not need key affinity. It can respond to live load more directly than a deterministic hash.
